# My plan for this year

I'm going to think through this the way I do every year — what went OK last season, what I can afford, and how to get three cabbage crops in without running myself and my family into the ground.

## My situation

Fifty mu of cabbage is a lot for one man, even with my wife helping. I'm 35, been at this five years now — long enough to know what kills a crop but not long enough to think I've seen everything. Around here the big wheat-maize farmers think we vegetable guys are crazy, but cabbage brings in more yuan per mu if you do it right, and my land is good for it. The well is what makes this possible — no well, no three crops.

Three crops of cabbage on the same land, same year. That's the system. Spring planting (transplant in February from seedlings I buy — I don't run a greenhouse myself), summer crop going in right after, then the autumn/winter crop for the big market. Each turnaround is maybe a week, and I have to be ready.

## How I think about this

My neighbor Old Wang has been at this fifteen years and he does about the same rotation. I watch what he does — last year he switched to a newer hybrid for the autumn crop and got better heads, so I'm going to try that too on maybe half my field. Not all of it, because if the new variety disappoints I still have the old one I know.

Fertilizer — the extension station tells us cabbage wants about 25 kg N per mu, plus potassium because cabbage is a potassium eater. I usually do a bit more than they say because a bad head means nothing at market, and the cost of an extra bag is less than the loss of one mu of undersized cabbage. I split it: base fertilizer before transplant (compound + some manure when I can get it from the chicken farm down the road), then one or two topdressings as the heads form.

Pests are the problem that keeps me awake. Cabbage worm, diamondback moth, aphids — especially in summer. You cannot skip spraying on cabbage. I probably spray four or five times per crop in summer, less in spring and autumn when it's cooler. This is where a lot of my cash goes.

Labor — my wife and I can't do 50 mu of transplanting or harvesting by ourselves. I hire village women for those peak weeks. Transplanting maybe 15 days of hired labor per crop, harvest another 10-15. That's real money but there's no way around it.

Market is the thing I can't control. Last autumn the price crashed because everyone in the county planted cabbage. I lost money on that crop. This year I'm going to try to stagger my planting a little — not all my cabbage ready the same week as everyone else's. Old Wang says the trick is to be a bit earlier or a bit later than the crowd.
